It is a Grade I listed building and a scheduled monument.
The site is owned by the National Trust but managed by English Heritage. There is a museum on the site holding many artefacts from the Abbey.

'''Hailes Abbey''' is a former [[Cistercian]] abbey, in the small village of [[Hailes, Gloucestershire|Hailes]], two miles northeast of [[Winchcombe]], [[Gloucestershire]], [[England]].  It was founded in 1246 as a daughter establishment of [[Beaulieu Abbey]] in [[Hampshire]]. The abbey was dissolved by [[Henry VIII]] in 1539. Little remains of the abbey. It is a Grade I [[listed building]]<ref>{{NHLE|desc=Hailes Abbey|num= 1154262 |access-date=16 August 2019}}</ref> and a [[scheduled monument]].<ref>{{NHLE|desc=Hailes Abbey and ringwork|num=1018070|access-date=16 August 2019}}</ref>

The site is owned by the [[National Trust]] but managed by [[English Heritage]]. There is a museum on the site holding many artefacts from the Abbey.

==History==
[[File:Boss of Samson at Hailes Abbey 2019-06-09.jpg|thumb|[[Boss (architecture)|Boss]] of [[Samson]] wrestling a lion, from Hailes Abbey]]
The abbey was founded in 1246 by [[Richard of Cornwall]], the younger brother of [[Henry III of England|Henry III]]. Richard was elected by the German Princes as [[Holy Roman Emperor]] but [[Pope Alexander IV]] refused him use of the title, henceforth he was styled [[King of the Romans]].<ref name=NT>[http://www.english-heritage.org.uk/hailes-abbey/ "Hailes Abbey"], ''English Heritage''.</ref> Richard founded the abbey to thank God after surviving a shipwreck.<ref name=EH>[https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/places/hailes-abbey/ "Hailes Abbey"], ''English Heritage''.</ref> Richard had been granted the manor of Hailes by King Henry, and settled it with a group of twenty Cistercian monks and ten [[lay brother]]s, led by Prior Jordan, from Beaulieu Abbey in Hampshire.<ref name="Guide">{{cite book |last1=Coad |first1=J G |title=Hailes Abbey |date=2001 |publisher=English Heritage |isbn=1-85074-466-1 |pages=17–22}}</ref><ref name=PS>{{PastScape|mnumber=328158 |mname=Hailes Abbey|access-date=14 June 2013}}</ref>  The great Cistercian abbey was entirely built in a single campaign in 1277, and was consecrated in a royal ceremony that included the King and [[Eleanor of Provence|Queen]] and 15 bishops. It was one of the last Cistercian houses to be founded in England.<ref name=Guide />

Hailes Abbey became a site of pilgrimage after Richard's son [[Edmund, 2nd Earl of Cornwall|Edmund]] donated to the Cistercian community a phial of the [[Blood of Christ|Holy Blood]], purchased in Germany, in 1270. Such a relic of the Crucifixion was a considerable magnet for [[pilgrimage]]. From the proceeds, the monks of Hailes were able to rebuild the Abbey on a magnificent scale.<ref name=PS/> One Abbot of Hailes was executed as a rebel after the [[Battle of Bramham Moor]], in 1408.<ref>{{cite web |title=War of the Roses in Yorkshire |date=12 June 2017 |url=https://www.yorkshire.com/inspiration/heritage/yorkshire-battlefields/war-of-the-roses-in-yorkshire |publisher=Yorkshire.com |access-date=2 July 2020}}</ref>

Though King Henry VIII's commissioners declared the famous relic to be nothing but the blood of a duck,<ref>{{cite web |title=The Holy Blood of Hailes |url=https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/places/hailes-abbey/history-and-stories/the-holy-blood-of-hailes/ |publisher=English Heritage |access-date=27 October 2019}}</ref> regularly renewed, and though the Abbot, Stephen Sagar, admitted that the Holy Blood was a fake in hope of saving the Abbey, Hailes Abbey was one of the last religious institutions to acquiesce following the [[Suppression of Religious Houses Act 1535]]. The Abbot and his monks finally surrendered their abbey to Henry's commissioners on Christmas Eve 1539.<ref name=PS/>

Following the Dissolution, the west range consisting of the Abbot's own apartments was converted into a house and was home to the Tracy family in the seventeenth century, but these buildings were later demolished and now all that remains are a few low arches in a meadow with outlines in the grass. Surviving remains include the small church for the disappeared parish, with unrestored medieval wall-paintings.<ref name=PS/>

In 1937 the site was donated to the National Trust  and in 1948 the [[Ministry of Works (United Kingdom)|Ministry of Works]], a predecessor of [[English Heritage]], assumed responsibility for the abbey.<ref name="Guide"/>

==Burials==
Among those buried at the Abbey were the founder, Richard of Cornwall, his second wife, [[Sanchia of Provence]], and his sons, [[Edmund, 2nd Earl of Cornwall]] and [[Henry of Almain]].<ref name=DW>{{cite book |last1=Winkless |first1=Doreen |title=Hailes Abbey |date=1990 |publisher=Speddon Press |location=Northumberland |isbn=1 871739 14 4 |page=5 |edition=2001}}</ref>

Outside the remains of the Abbey is Hailes Church.  The church is older than the abbey, and was consecrated in 1175.  It later served as the ''capella ante portas'' (Latin for 'chapel outside the gates') to the Abbey until the Abbey's [[Dissolution of the monasteries|dissolution]] in 1539.  Inside the church are fine 14th-century wall paintings depicting St Catherine and St Christopher, on the north wall, and St Margaret and coursing scenes, on the south.<ref name=DW /> The church is also a Grade I listed building.<ref>{{National Heritage List for England|num=1154315|desc=Church (dedication unknown), Stanway|grade=I}}</ref> The church is part of the Eastern Parishes benefice, north of Winchcombe, and occasional services are held.<ref>{{cite web |title=Hailes Church |url=https://www.winchcombeparish.org.uk/the-wider-team/eastern-group-of-churches/hailes-church/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151004121349/http://www.winchcombeparish.org.uk/the-wider-team/eastern-group-of-churches/hailes-church/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=4 October 2015 |website=Winchcombeparish.org.uk |access-date=20 May 2020 }}</ref>

'''Bibury''' is a village and [[Civil parishes in England|civil parish]] in [[Gloucestershire]], England. It is on the [[River Coln]], a [[River Thames|Thames]] tributary that rises in the [[Cotswolds]]. The village centre is {{convert|6|mi|km|0|abbr=off}} northeast of [[Cirencester]]. [[Arlington Row]] is a nationally notable [[traditional architecture|architectural]] [[conservation area]] depicted on the inside cover of some [[British passport]]s. It is a major destination for tourists visiting the traditional rural villages, [[tea houses]] and many [[Grade I listed buildings in Cotswold (district)|historic buildings]] of the [[Cotswold District]]; it is one of six places in the country featured in [[Mini-Europe]], [[Brussels]].

==History==
[[File:Bibury Church - geograph.org.uk - 1107679.jpg|thumb|left|upright|St Mary's Church, Bibury]]
In the ''[[Domesday Book]]'' (1086), a record of survey done under [[William the Conqueror]], the place is named ''Becheberie'', and it is recorded that the lands and church in Bibury were held by [[Worcester Cathedral|St Mary's Priory]] at [[Worcester, England|Worcester]], from whom it passed in 1130 to [[Osney Abbey]], near [[Oxford]]: the Abbey continued to hold it until its [[Dissolution of the Monasteries|dissolution]] in 1540.<ref>{{cite book |last=Croome |first=W.I. |title=A Short History of St Mary's Bibury |year=1992 |location=Gloucester |publisher=The British Printing Company Ltd |oclc=78092632}}</ref>

The [[Church of England parish church|Church of England]] [[Church of St Mary, Bibury|Church of St Mary]] is very late [[Anglo-Saxon architecture|Anglo-Saxon]] with later additions and listed in the top of the three heritage/architecture categories, Grade I. Its main material is random ([[cobblestone]]) and [[ashlar|coursed]] rubble limestone with a slate roof. It is formed of a nave with north and south aisles, south porch, north west tower and chancel, tower, arched doorways.<ref>{{NHLE|num=1155770|desc=Bibury Church|grade=I|accessdate=27 January 2015}}</ref><ref name="Verey1970">{{cite book |last=Verey |first=David |title=[[The Buildings of England]]: Gloucestershire: The Cotswolds |year=1970 |publisher=[[Penguin Books]] |location=Harmondsworth |isbn=0-14-071040-X |pages=106–112}}</ref> The churchyard has been described as being "of special interest because of the remarkable survival of so many excellently carved table tombs with bale tops, and headstones with cherubs and symbolic figures of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries".<ref>{{cite book |first=David |last=Verey |title=Cotswold Churches |publisher=B. T. Batsford Ltd. |date=1976 |page=94 |isbn=978-1845880286}}</ref> There is an early [[canonical sundial]] on the south wall. From AD 1130 until the [[English Reformation]] during the 16th century, the church was a [[Royal Peculiar|peculier]] of [[Osney Abbey]] in [[Oxford]].<ref name="Verey1970"/>

Adjacent to the church is the village primary school that was built in the 1850s. In 2023 the school had 27 pupils in two classes.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://reports.ofsted.gov.uk/provider/21/146812 |title=Bibury Church of England Primary School:OFSTED Report 2023|access-date=25 March 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250120224842/https://reports.ofsted.gov.uk/provider/21/146812 |archive-date=20 January 2025|url-status=live}}</ref> On the Arlington (west) side of the village is Arlington [[Baptist]] Church, where a congregation has been meeting since the 1740s.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.arlingtonbaptist.org.uk/index.html |title=Arlington Baptist Church Website |publisher=Arlington Baptist Church |access-date=7 August 2013 |archive-date=22 July 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130722220847/http://arlingtonbaptist.org.uk/index.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

Late in the 19th century George Witts recounted the discovery of the Bibury [[Roman villa]]: "In the year 1880 a [[Roman villa]] was accidentally discovered in the parish of Bibury, about {{convert|6|mi|km|0|abbr=off}} northeast of [[Cirencester]]. Some Roman [[pottery]], [[coin]]s, remnants of [[Floor mosaic|tesselated pavements]], &c., were found, but as no examination has yet taken place, no description of the building can be given."—George Witts, 1883.<ref name="Witts1883">{{cite book|last=Witts|first=George|title=Archaeological Handbook of the County of Gloucester|year=1883|publisher=G. Norman|location=Cheltenham|url=https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Gazetteer/Places/Europe/Great_Britain/England/Gloucestershire/_Texts/WITGLO*/Villas.html#1|access-date=6 November 2009|archive-date=2 May 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210502173946/https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Gazetteer/Places/Europe/Great_Britain/England/Gloucestershire/_Texts/WITGLO%2A/Villas.html#1|url-status=live}}</ref> The site fills a small low meander downstream of the bridge on the Arlington, Bibury side.<ref>[[Scheduled Ancient Monument]] official listing. {{NHLE|num=1003357|desc=Site of Roman Villa near Bibury Mill|accessdate=27 January 2015}}</ref> Bibury village [[nucleated village|proper]], on the east bank, consists of approximately 40 homes and businesses, of which two are prominent hotels.

==Visitor attractions==
[[File:Arlington Mill in Bibury - geograph.org.uk - 1440332.jpg|thumb|Arlington Mill in Bibury in 2009]]
The 19th-century [[Arts and Crafts movement|artist and craftsman]] [[William Morris]] called Bibury "the most beautiful village in England" when he visited it.<ref>{{cite book|last=Gibbs|first=J.A.|title=A Cotswold Village|year=1898|publisher=VCH Glos|page=23}}</ref><ref name=bbc/>

The village is known for its honey-coloured 17th-century stone cottages with steeply pitched roofs, which once housed [[weaving|weavers]] who supplied cloth for [[fulling]] at nearby Arlington Mill. Until the 1980s, that building also housed the museum of Arlington Mill with a collection of period clothing, before it was shifted to Barnsley House.<ref name=bbc>{{cite web | title = Gloucestershire - History - Day Out: The South East Cotswolds | url = https://www.bbc.co.uk/gloucestershire/content/articles/2008/10/23/dayout_se_cotswolds_video_feature.shtml | publisher = BBC | date = Jan 2009 | access-date = 7 August 2013 | archive-date = 13 November 2012 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20121113090337/http://www.bbc.co.uk/gloucestershire/content/articles/2008/10/23/dayout_se_cotswolds_video_feature.shtml | url-status = live }}</ref> The Mill is now a private residence.<ref>{{cite news|title=Top 15 unusual buildings for sale: 02|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/property/buyingsellingandmoving/9775390/Top-15-unusual-buildings-for-sale.html|newspaper=Daily Telegraph|access-date=4 April 2018|archive-date=18 December 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141218183252/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/property/buyingsellingandmoving/9775390/Top-15-unusual-buildings-for-sale.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>
{{multiple image
| align     =left
| direction = vertical
| image1    =Bibury Cottages.jpg
|caption1=Bibury cottages
|image2=Bibury Court.jpg
|caption2= Bibury Court, built in 1633

The place where the wool was hung to dry after being washed in Arlington Row, was known as "Rack Isle". Today, this water meadow and marshy area, which is seasonally flooded and surrounded by [[water]] from three sides, is an important habitat for water-loving plants and birds including [[mallard]]s, [[Eurasian coot|coot]]s, and [[Common moorhen|moorhen]]s; it is also a National Trust Wildfowl Reserve.<ref name="nationaltrust"/><ref name="bbcd">{{cite web | title = Domesday Reloaded: Wildlife On Rack Isle, Bibury | url = http://www.bbc.co.uk/history/domesday/dblock/GB-408000-204000/page/5 | publisher = BBC | access-date = 7 August 2013 | archive-date = 25 September 2015 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20150925061233/http://www.bbc.co.uk/history/domesday/dblock/GB-408000-204000/page/5 | url-status = dead }}</ref>

Bibury is particularly frequented by Japanese tourists; this is largely attributed to emperor [[Hirohito]] having stayed in the village on his European tour.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NtkCnODXfH8C&q=emperor+hirohito+bibury&pg=PT637|title=Frommer's England and the Best of Wales|first1=Nick|last1=Dalton|publisher=Wiley|date=2012|isbn=9781118331378|access-date=8 November 2020|archive-date=2 May 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210502173945/https://books.google.com/books?id=NtkCnODXfH8C&q=emperor+hirohito+bibury&pg=PT637|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="gloucestershireecho.co.uk">{{cite web |url=http://www.gloucestershireecho.co.uk/Passport-picture-influx-tourists-according-Bibury/story-21747410-detail/story.html |title=Passport picture not behind influx of tourists according to Bibury residents | Gloucestershire Echo |access-date=2014-08-04 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140808042758/http://www.gloucestershireecho.co.uk/Passport-picture-influx-tourists-according-Bibury/story-21747410-detail/story.html |archive-date=8 August 2014 |df=dmy-all }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://biburyshop.blogspot.co.uk/2010/05/japanese-and-english.html |title=Tales from Bibury Shop: Japanese and English |access-date=4 August 2014 |archive-date=18 December 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141218193816/http://biburyshop.blogspot.co.uk/2010/05/japanese-and-english.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

The largest building in Bibury is [[Bibury Court]], built in 1633 in the [[Jacobean architecture|Jacobean]] style,<ref name="telegraphrw">{{cite news | author = Fiona Duncan | title = Bibury Court hotel, Cotswolds, Gloucestershire: review | url = https://www.telegraph.co.uk/travel/hotel/79144/Bibury-Court-hotel-Cotswolds-Gloucestershire-review.html | newspaper = The Telegraph | access-date = 7 August 2013 | archive-date = 1 October 2015 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20151001072338/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/travel/hotel/79144/Bibury-Court-hotel-Cotswolds-Gloucestershire-review.html | url-status = live }}</ref> and lived in by [[James Dutton, 3rd Baron Sherborne|Lord Sherborne]] during the nineteenth century. It is now a Grade I [[listed building]], and was a [[hotel]] from 1968 to 2014, when it closed.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Archer |first1=Megan |title=Bibury Court Hotel to be transformed into large country house due to business decline |url=https://www.wiltsglosstandard.co.uk/news/11673370.bibury-court-hotel-to-be-transformed-into-large-country-house-due-to-business-decline/ |access-date=2 May 2021 |work=Wilts and Gloucestershire Standard |date=18 December 2014 |archive-date=3 March 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200303174208/https://www.wiltsglosstandard.co.uk/news/11673370.bibury-court-hotel-to-be-transformed-into-large-country-house-due-to-business-decline/ |url-status=live }}</ref> It was then purchased by the designer [[Marc Newson]] to be his family home.<ref>{{Cite web |date=7 June 2022|title=Designer Marc Newson's offshore inspiration |url=https://www.afr.com/rear-window/designer-marc-newson-s-offshore-inspiration-20220607-p5arp0 |access-date=25 March 2025 |website=Australian Financial Review}}</ref>

===Arlington Row===
The picturesque [[Arlington Row]] cottages were built in 1380 as a monastic wool store. This was converted into a row of cottages for weavers in the 17th century.<ref name="nationaltrust">{{cite web | title = Bibury | url = http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/bibury/ | publisher = National Trust | access-date = 7 August 2013 | archive-date = 3 August 2013 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20130803234657/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/bibury/ | url-status = live }}</ref> The cloth produced there was sent to Arlington Mill. Arlington Row is a popular visitor attraction,<ref name=bbc/> probably one of the most photographed Cotswold scenes,{{according to whom?|date=March 2025}} and was preserved by the [[Royal College of Arts]]. It has been used as a film and television location, most notably for the film ''[[Stardust (2007 film)|Stardust]]''. Claims that ''[[Bridget Jones's Diary (film)|Bridget Jones's Diary]]'' was also filmed at Arlington Row seem incorrect.<ref name="bibury.com">{{cite web | title = Arlington Row on the Bibury Website | url = https://www.bibury.com/arlington-row/ }}</ref><ref name="gloucestershireecho.co.uk"/><ref>IMDB Website</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.gloucestercitizen.co.uk/Beauty-spots-appear-new-passports/story-11931593-detail/story.html |title=Travellers who admire the stamps in their passports while waiting in line at airports will soon have views from the West to look at. | Gloucester Citizen |access-date=2014-08-04 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924022813/http://www.gloucestercitizen.co.uk/Beauty-spots-appear-new-passports/story-11931593-detail/story.html |archive-date=24 September 2015 |df=dmy-all }}</ref> In 2017 the BBC reported that an "ugly" car parked by an elderly resident had been vandalised, possibly by visitors who had repeatedly complained that it spoilt photographs.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-gloucestershire-38867290|title=Notorious yellow car vandalised in Bibury|work=BBC Gloucester|date=4 February 2017|access-date=4 February 2017|archive-date=4 February 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170204111506/http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-gloucestershire-38867290|url-status=live}}</ref>
{{clear}}

==Geography==
[[File:Swan Hotel Bibury.jpg|thumb|Grade II listed buildings in Bibury along the River Coln]]
The [[River Coln|Coln]], a tributary of the Thames, flows in a very steep valley (in [[Thames Basin]] terms) southeastwards.  It flows alongside the midsection of Bibury with Arlington's main street which [[wikt:dogleg|dogleg]]s to achieve this.  Each side has a similar concentration and scale of development; each bank's development falls mainly in the Bibury [[conservation area]] which has an insightful district surveyor's statement for building owners and visitors.<ref>[http://www.cotswold.gov.uk/residents/planning-building/historic-buildings-conservation-areas/conservation-areas/ Documents related to Bibury Conservation Area] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170513010041/http://www.cotswold.gov.uk/residents/planning-building/historic-buildings-conservation-areas/conservation-areas/ |date=13 May 2017 }} Retrieved 27 January 2015</ref>

The parish is approximately rectangular and stretches far to the rolling, elevated, north. It includes on outlying settlement, [[Ablington, Gloucestershire|Ablington]], in the upper valley. Bibury Farm is {{convert|300|m|yd}} from the village, {{convert|151|m}} above [[Ordnance Datum]] (AOD), which is a similar elevation to much of the north. The south rises to a maximum of {{convert|141|m}} on its periphery along [[Akeman Street]], a Roman road, before ascending further in other more distant lands. The valley floor within the Bibury boundary, northwest and southeast, ranges from {{convert|108|to|98|m}} AOD.{{Citation needed|date=July 2022}}

The Coln, along with the Bibury Spring, supplies Bibury [[Trout]] farm, founded in 1902 by the naturalist Arthur Severn, to stock the local rivers and streams with the native [[brown trout]]. The hatchery spawns up to six million trout ova every year.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.biburytroutfarm.co.uk/ |title=Bibury Trout Farm Website |publisher=Biburytroutfarm.co.uk |access-date=7 August 2013 |archive-date=6 August 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130806102845/http://www.biburytroutfarm.co.uk/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Three medieval [[dispersed village|clusters]] are all interspersed by substantial grass, making for a dense developed area compared to suburbs but not in terms of roads; a footbridge connects both sides (Arlington and Bibury) as well as various footpaths in all directions. Elevations vary widely even throughout the village parts, with the gentlest slope in the eastern escarpment of the [[Cotswold Hills]] for {{convert|1|mi|km|round=0.5|abbr=off}} or more in each direction taken by the main village road.{{Citation needed|date=July 2022}}

==Culture==
The world's first [[horse racing]] club, The Bibury Club, was formed in 1681 and held race meetings on Macaroni Downs above the village until the early 20th century.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://thecotswoldgateway.co.uk/horseracing.htm |title=The CotsWolds:Horse Racing |publisher=Thecotswoldgateway.co.uk |access-date=7 August 2013 |archive-date=24 March 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120324141249/http://thecotswoldgateway.co.uk/horseracing.htm |url-status=live }}</ref>

==In popular media==
Bibury is prominently featured as a character's hometown in the [[manga]] series ''[[Kin-iro Mosaic]]''. The director of its animated adaptation, Motoki "Tensho" Tanaka, later founded [[Bibury Animation Studios]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://bibury-st.com/|title=company|website=bibury-st.com|language=ja|date=February 17, 2020}}</ref>

==Notable inhabitants==
In 2000, [[Daniel Brennan]] KC, barrister, was made [[Baron Brennan|Lord Brennan]] and Bibury is his [[territorial designation]] as his home village.<ref>{{London Gazette |issue=55839 |date=5 May 2000|page=4980 }}</ref> 

The merchant and writer [[Thomas Tryon]] was a native of Bibury.<ref>{{cite book |last=Stuart |first=Tristram |title=[[The Bloodless Revolution (book)|The Bloodless Revolution: Radical Vegetarianism and the Discovery of India ]] |publisher=Harper Collins |location=London |date=2006 |page=60 |isbn=978-0-00-712892-1}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Spencer |first=Colin |title=The Heretic's Feast. A History of Vegetarianism |publisher=Fourth Estate |location=London |date=1993 |page=206 |isbn=1857020782}}</ref>

2095226.title: Northey Island
2095226.extract:
Northey Island is an island in the estuary of the River Blackwater, Essex. It is linked to the south bank of the river by a causeway, covered for up to 3 hours either side of high tide.  The island is approximately 1 mile (2 km) to the east of Maldon, Essex and 1 mile (2 km) to the west of Osea Island.
The island is owned by the National Trust. For accurate information on visiting safely, saltmarsh creation and managed realignment go to www.nationaltrust.org.uk/northey-island
The Battle of Maldon, 991 is believed to have taken place on the causeway and the south bank of the Blackwater near the island. At that time the causeway is thought to have been half as long as it is presently – 120 yards rather than 240 yards today.
Significant land reclamation was carried out by the Dutch contractor Nicholas Van Cropenrough in the early 18th century; he unwalled marshland to significantly enlarge the island but the walls were breached by the sea and the land returned to marshland on 29 November 1897.
In 1923 Northey was bought by the writer and campaigner Norman Angell; in 1933 he was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.
The island is part of the Blackwater Estuary Site of Special Scientific Interest. Northey is home to diverse birdlife and this is reflected in the place name 'Awl Creek' which perpetuates the traditional Essex dialect word for the Avocet.
At one time Northey was home to more species than it is now. The island was one of the last southern strongholds of the raven, the last bird being taken from the Ladies grove in 1888.
It is one of 43 (unbridged) tidal islands which can be walked to from the British mainland and one of six such tidal islands in Essex.

The island is part of the Blackwater Estuary Site of Special Scientific Interest. Northey is home to diverse birdlife and this is reflected in the place name 'Awl Creek' which perpetuates the traditional Essex dialect word for the [[Avocet]].<ref name=countrylife/>

At one time Northey was home to more species than it is now. The island was one of the last southern strongholds of the [[raven]], the last bird being taken from the Ladies grove in 1888.<ref name=countrylife/>

It is one of 43 (unbridged) tidal islands which can be walked to from the [[UK|British]] mainland and one of six such tidal islands in Essex.<ref>No Boat Required – Exploring Tidal Islands, Peter Caton, 2011, Troubador Publishing, {{ISBN|978-1848767-010}}</ref>

4567790.title: Dyrham Park
4567790.extract:
Dyrham Park () is a baroque English country house in an ancient deer park near the village of Dyrham in South Gloucestershire, England. The house, with the attached orangery and stable block, is a Grade I listed building, while the park is Grade II* listed on the National Register of Historic Parks and Gardens.
The current house was built for William Blathwayt in stages during the 17th and early 18th centuries on the site of a previous manor house, with the final façade being designed by William Talman. It contains art works and furniture from around the world, particularly Holland, and includes a collection of Dutch Masters. The house is linked to the 13th-century church of St Peter, also Grade I listed, where many of the Blathwayt family are buried. The house is surrounded by 274 acres (111 ha) of formal gardens, and parkland which supports a herd of fallow deer. The grounds, which were originally laid out by George London and later developed by Charles Harcourt Masters, include water features and statuary.
The house and estate are now owned by the National Trust and underwent extensive renovation in 2014 and 2015. They are open to the public and host events and attractions, including open-air concerts. They have also been used as a location for film and television productions.

main.*:
{{Short description|Country house and park in Gloucestershire, England, United Kingdom}} {{for|the house and golf club in Hertfordshire|Dyrham Park Country Club}} {{good article}} {{Use dmy dates|date=August 2016}} {{Use British English|date=February 2023}} {{Infobox historic site | name = Dyrham Park | image = Dyrham Park lower park.jpg | caption = Lower part of the park and east front of the house and orangery | type = [[English country house|Country house]] | locmapin = Gloucestershire | coordinates = {{coord|51.4801|-2.3734|type:landmark_region:GB-SGC|format=dms|display=inline,title}} | gbgridref = ST742757 | location = [[Dyrham and Hinton]], [[Gloucestershire]] | built = 1692-1704 | architect = {{ubl|Samuel Hauduroy|[[William Talman (architect)|William Talman]]}} | architecture = [[Baroque]] | owner = [[National Trust]] | designation1 = Grade I | designation1_offname = Dyrham House | designation1_date = 17 Sep 1952 | designation1_number = {{listed building England|1212039}} | designation2 = National Register of Historic Parks and Gardens | designation2_offname = Dyrham Park | designation2_date = 30 Apr 1987 | designation2_number = {{listed building England|1000443}} }} '''Dyrham Park''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|d|ɪ|r|əm}}) is a [[baroque]] [[English country house]] in an ancient deer park near the village of [[Dyrham]] in [[South Gloucestershire]], England. The house, with the attached orangery and stable block, is a Grade I [[Listed building#Categories of listed building|listed building]], while the park is Grade II* listed on the [[Register of Historic Parks and Gardens of special historic interest in England|National Register of Historic Parks and Gardens]]. The current house was built for [[William Blathwayt]] in stages during the 17th and early 18th centuries on the site of a previous manor house, with the final façade being designed by [[William Talman (architect)|William Talman]]. It contains art works and furniture from around the world, particularly Holland, and includes a collection of [[Dutch Golden Age painting|Dutch Masters]]. The house is linked to the 13th-century church of St Peter, also Grade I listed, where many of the Blathwayt family are buried. The house is surrounded by {{convert|274|acre}} of formal gardens, and parkland which supports a herd of [[fallow deer]]. The grounds, which were originally laid out by [[George London (landscape architect)|George London]] and later developed by [[Charles Harcourt Masters]], include water features and statuary. The house and estate are now owned by the [[National Trust]] and underwent extensive renovation in 2014 and 2015. They are open to the public and host events and attractions, including open-air concerts. They have also been used as a location for film and television productions. ==History== [[File:DyrhamLicence1511.jpg|thumb|left|upright=0.8|Royal licence to empark Dyrham granted by [[Henry VIII]] to [[William Denys]], [[Esquire of the Body]], 5 June 1511. Attached is a rare perfect example of the Great Seal of Henry VIII. Collection of Dyrham Park, National Trust]] The [[Manor of Dyrham]] has been recorded since the [[Domesday Book]] of 1086, when there were 34 households.{{OpenDomesday|OS=ST7475|name=dyrham|display=Dyrham}} The first lord of the manor to be resident may have been [[William Denys]], who was an [[Esquire of the Body]] to [[Henry VIII]] and later [[High Sheriff of Gloucestershire]]. He was granted the [[Deer park (England)#Licence to empark|licence to empark]] {{convert|500|acre}} of Dyrham in 1511, although not all of this area was enclosed.{{cite web|title=Dyrham Park, Dyrham and Hinton, Near Bath, England|url=http://www.parksandgardens.org/places-and-people/site/1194?preview=1|publisher=Parks and Gardens UK|access-date=26 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160827175518/http://www.parksandgardens.org/places-and-people/site/1194?preview=1|archive-date=27 August 2016|url-status=live}} This meant that he could enclose the land with a wall or hedge bank and maintain a captive herd of deer within the park, over which he had exclusive hunting rights; the name "Dyrham" is derived from the Anglo-Saxon word ''dirham'', an enclosure for deer.{{cite book |title=The Oxford Dictionary of English Place Names |last=Ekwall |year=1960 |publisher=Oxford |page=155 }} The estate was sold to the Wynter family in 1571 and Sir George Wynter was allowed to empark further land in 1620. [[File:Dyrham Park eagle.jpg|thumb|Eagle sculpture on the roof of Dyrham Park]] In 1689, the estate was acquired through marriage by [[William Blathwayt]], who was [[Secretary at War]] to [[William III of England|William III]]. He retained the existing Tudor building and expanded it in stages.{{cite book|last1=Garnett|first1=Oliver|title=Dyrham Park|date=2000|publisher=National Trust|isbn=978-1843590965|pages=28–29}} The west front of 1692 was commissioned from [[Huguenot]] architect Samuel Hauduroy, and includes an [[Italianate architecture|Italianate]] double staircase leading from the terrace to the grounds. In 1698, a stable block was added with space for 26 horses and servants' quarters above around a courtyard. The east front of 1704 was designed by [[William Talman (architect)|William Talman]], architect of [[Chatsworth House|Chatsworth]].{{NHLE|desc=Dyrham House|num=1212039|access-date=15 November 2019}} The construction of the east wing included demolition of the remains of the original Tudor house and the addition of a statue of an eagle on the roof. Dyrham next became a showcase of Dutch decorative arts.{{cite web|title=A View through a House|url=http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/453733|website=National Trust Collections|publisher=National Trust|access-date=31 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161012054728/http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/453733|archive-date=12 October 2016|url-status=live}}{{cite web|title=History of Dyrham Park|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/dyrham-park/features/history-of-dyrham-park|publisher=National Trust|access-date=31 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160919033739/https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/dyrham-park/features/history-of-dyrham-park|archive-date=19 September 2016|url-status=live}} The collection includes [[delftware]], paintings, and furniture. Eighteenth-century additions include furniture by [[Waring & Gillow|Gillow]] and [[John Linnell (cabinet maker)|Linnell]]. The interiors have remained little altered since decorated by Blathwayt. The gardens were designed by [[George London (landscape architect)|George London]] in the late 17th and early 18th centuries.{{cite web|title=Dyrham Park, Dyrham and Hinton, Near Bath, England|url=http://www.parksandgardens.org/places-and-people/site/1194/history|website=Parks and Gardens UK|publisher=Parks and Gardens Data Services Ltd|access-date=26 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160827174201/http://www.parksandgardens.org/places-and-people/site/1194/history|archive-date=27 August 2016|url-status=dead}} [[File:Dyrham Park roof.jpg|thumb|Roof repairs viewed from the walkway]] The Blathwayt family owned the house until 1956, when the government acquired it. During the [[Second World War]] it was used for child evacuees while rented by Anne, [[Baroness]] Islington, the widow of [[John Dickson-Poynder, 1st Baron Islington]] (1866-1936), a former [[Governor of New Zealand]]. Lady Islington redecorated many of the rooms.{{cite book|last1=Garnett|first1=Oliver|title=Dyrham Park|date=2000|publisher=National Trust|isbn=978-1843590965|page=32}}{{cite web|title=History talk focuses on wartime nursery and children's homes|url=https://info.uwe.ac.uk/news/uwenews/news.aspx?id=1142|publisher=University of the West of England|access-date=12 September 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160625152753/http://info.uwe.ac.uk/news/uwenews/news.aspx?id=1142|archive-date=25 June 2016|url-status=live}} The National Trust acquired it in 1961. In 2015, major renovation work included replacing the roof. Part of the cost was met from a [[Heritage Lottery Fund]] grant of £85,000.{{cite web|title=Dyrham Park secures Heritage Lottery Fund investment|url=http://www.ntsouthwest.co.uk/2014/10/dyrham-park-secures-heritage-lottery-fund-investment/|publisher=National Trust|access-date=27 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160924063911/http://www.ntsouthwest.co.uk/2014/10/dyrham-park-secures-heritage-lottery-fund-investment/|archive-date=24 September 2016|url-status=live}} While the repairs were in progress, visitors could view the house from a rooftop walkway.{{cite news |title=Dyrham Park aerial walkway to view roof replacement work |work=BBC News |date=6 May 2015 |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-somerset-32587115 |access-date=1 July 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161211044226/http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-somerset-32587115 |archive-date=11 December 2016 |url-status=live }}{{cite web|title=Dyrham Mansion near Bath|url=http://integral-engineering.co.uk/projects/conservation/dyrham/|publisher=Integral Engineering|access-date=27 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160828034503/http://integral-engineering.co.uk/projects/conservation/dyrham/|archive-date=28 August 2016|url-status=live}} In 2020, the National Trust published a report which examined the connections of its properties to the [[British Empire]]. The report's authors noted that Dyrham Park was owned by several individuals who were involved in administering colonies, including Blathwayt, who was a prominent official in the [[Southern Department (Great Britain)|Southern Department]].{{Cite magazine| url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2021/08/23/britains-idyllic-country-houses-reveal-a-darker-history |title=Britain's Idyllic Country Houses Reveal a Darker History| magazine=[[The New Yorker]] |date=13 August 2021}}[https://nt.global.ssl.fastly.net/binaries/content/assets/website/national/pdf/colonialism-and-historic-slavery-report.pdf Interim Report on the Connections between Colonialism and Properties now in the Care of the National Trust, Including Links with Historic Slavery] ==Architecture== ===House=== [[File:Dyrham Park garden.jpg|thumb|left|Dyrham Park west front and garden]] The [[limestone]] building has [[slate]] and [[lead]] roofs above the attics. The two-storey west front, which was built in the 1690s, has three [[Bay (architecture)|bays]] of each side of the central doorway, which has [[Doric order|Doric]] columns, with smaller pavilions at the ends of the wings. One of the wings creates a covered passageway to the church of St Peter. The east front, which was added around 1704, has shallow projecting wings and a central door under a [[balustrade]] with an [[Italianate architecture|Italianate]] double staircase leading down to the lawns. A central [[pedestal]] is inscribed "virtute et veritate". Above it is an eagle statue, carved by John Harvey of Bath, representing the family crest of the Blathwayt family. [[File:View of a Corridor 1662 Samuel van Hoogstraten.jpg|thumb|upright=0.6|"View of a Corridor" painted in 1662 by [[Samuel Dirksz van Hoogstraten]]]] The interior is sumptuously decorated with wood panelling and tiles of [[Delftware]]. The collection of artworks and artifacts includes furniture, [[Porcelain|china]] and pictures with a strong Dutch influence.{{cite web|title=Dyrham Park, Gloucestershire (Accredited Museum)|url=http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/place/dyrham-park|publisher=National Trust|access-date=26 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160727205904/http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/place/dyrham-park|archive-date=27 July 2016|url-status=live}} The china includes a pair of [[tulip vase]]s made in the 1680s.{{cite book|last1=Garnett|first1=Oliver|title=Dyrham Park|date=2000|publisher=National Trust|isbn=978-1843590965|page=14}} The state bed, with crimson and yellow velvet hangings, was made in Anglo-Dutch style around 1704. The entrance hall is hung with bird paintings by [[Melchior d'Hondecoeter]] and throughout the house are landscape and still lifes by [[Abraham Storck]], [[Samuel Dirksz van Hoogstraten]], [[David Teniers the Younger]], d'Hondecoeter, and other [[Dutch Golden Age painting|Dutch Masters]]. Hoogstratens "View of a Corridor" has been hung in a doorway as the artist originally intended.{{cite book|last1=Garnett|first1=Oliver|title=Dyrham Park|date=2000|publisher=National Trust|isbn=978-1843590965|page=12}} Blathwayt's travels are also represented by paintings by Spanish artists such as [[Bartolomé Esteban Murillo]] and a staircase made of [[walnut]] from his estates as auditor general of the [[Colony of Virginia]].{{cite book|last1=Garnett|first1=Oliver|title=Dyrham Park|date=2000|publisher=National Trust|isbn=978-1843590965|page=8}} Many of these were brought to Dyrham by George William Blathwayt after he inherited the house in 1844. There are also artifacts from Blathwayt's journeys to other parts of the world, particularly Jamaica.{{cite book|last1=Nelson|first1=Louis|title=Architecture and Empire in Jamaica|date=2016|publisher=Yale University Press|isbn=9780300214352|page=237|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=P_2oCwAAQBAJ&dq=Dyrham+Park&pg=PA237|access-date=27 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160920134610/https://books.google.co.uk/books?id=P_2oCwAAQBAJ&pg=PA237&dq=Dyrham+Park&hl=en&sa=X&redir_esc=y#v=onepage&q=Dyrham%20Park&f=false|archive-date=20 September 2016|url-status=live}} ===Orangery and stable block=== On the south eastern side of the house is an [[orangery]], which was built as a [[greenhouse]] in 1701 and has a glazed roof which was added around 1800 by [[Humphrey Repton]].{{cite web|title=Orangery attached to south east of Dyrham House|url=https://www.historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1212042|website=National Heritage List for England|publisher=Historic England|access-date=27 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160827183908/https://www.historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1212042|archive-date=27 August 2016|url-status=live}} The orangery hides the view of the servants' quarters from the main house. The servants' quarters was revised and modernised in the 1840s. It contains the kitchen, dairy, bakehouse and several [[larder]]s for raw and cooked meat. There is also a servants' hall where the staff would take their meals and a tenants' hall which was used by the [[tenant farmer]]s to eat on the days when they came to pay their rent.{{cite book|last1=Garnett|first1=Oliver|title=Dyrham Park|date=2000|publisher=National Trust|isbn=978-1843590965|pages=18–20}} In addition to the designs for the house, William Talman created the large 15-bay stable block.{{cite web|title=Stable Block attached to south of Dyrham House|url=https://www.historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1289719|website=National Heritage List for England|publisher=Historic England|access-date=27 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160827180414/https://www.historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1289719|archive-date=27 August 2016|url-status=live}} It is now used as a tea-room for visitors.{{cite web|title=Dyrham Park tea-room|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/dyrham-park/features/dyrham-park-tea-room|publisher=National Trust|access-date=27 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160918152738/https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/dyrham-park/features/dyrham-park-tea-room|archive-date=18 September 2016|url-status=live}} ===Church=== {{Infobox historic site | name = St Peter's Church | image = St Peter's Church, Dyrham, from house lawn (cropped).jpg | designation1 = Grade I | designation1_offname = Church of St Peter

The church consists of a north and south [[aisle]], [[chancel]] and south west porch with the tower to the west.{{cite web|title=Church of St. Peter|url=https://www.historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1289711|website=National Heritage List for England|publisher=Historic England|access-date=27 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160827180222/https://www.historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1289711|archive-date=27 August 2016|url-status=live}} In the south [[aisle]] are [[encaustic tile]]s dating from the 13th century.{{cite web|title=The Wheel of Life|url=http://www.wanhs.org/CircleofLife.html|publisher=Weston-super-Mare Archaeological and Natural History Society|access-date=27 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170117020926/http://www.wanhs.org/CircleofLife.html|archive-date=17 January 2017|url-status=live}} The [[Baptismal font|font]] is [[Norman architecture|Norman]] while the [[pulpit]] is [[Jacobean architecture|Jacobean]]. The church is not owned by the National Trust but is closely associated with the rest of the estate and has the tombs and memorials for many owners of the house.{{cite web|title=St Peter's Dyrham|url=http://www.wickbenefice.net/dyrham|publisher=Wick Benefice|access-date=27 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160830135722/http://www.wickbenefice.net/dyrham|archive-date=30 August 2016|url-status=live}} The parish is part of the [[benefice]] of [[Downton, Wiltshire|Wick]] with [[Doynton]] and Dyrham, within the [[Diocese of Bristol]].{{cite web|title=St Peter, Dyrham|url=https://www.achurchnearyou.com/dyrham-st-peter/|website=A Church Near You|publisher=Church of England|access-date=27 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160828033647/https://www.achurchnearyou.com/dyrham-st-peter/|archive-date=28 August 2016|url-status=live}} ==Grounds== [[File:DyrhamKip.jpg|thumb|"Dyrham the Seat of William Blathwait Esq." It is one of the largest and most elaborate Roman villas so far discovered in Britain and one with the latest occupation beyond the Roman period. The villa was discovered in 1864, and was excavated and opened to public view soon afterwards. It was acquired in 1924 by the National Trust who have conducted a long-term conservation programme, with new on-site facilities and cover-buildings.
Historians have debated whether Chedworth was a villa rustica or a religious sanctuary and hostel, as evidence has been found in support of both arguments. Most currently believe, however, that Chedworth was the former, inhabited by a very wealthy Romano-Briton.

'''Chedworth Roman Villa''' is located near [[Chedworth]], [[Gloucestershire]], England<ref>{{cite web |url=http://pleiades.stoa.org/places/79383 |title=Places: 79383 (Chedworth) |author=Esmonde Cleary, A., DARMC, R. Talbert, J. Åhlfeldt, R. Warner, J. Becker, S. Gillies, T. Elliott |access-date=March 16, 2013<!-- 2:22 pm --> |publisher=Pleiades |archive-date=21 September 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130921135054/http://pleiades.stoa.org/places/79383 |url-status=live }}</ref> and is a [[scheduled monument]].<ref>{{NHLE|desc=Chedworth Roman Villa|num= 1003324 |accessdate=16 November 2018}}</ref> It is one of the largest and most elaborate [[Roman villa]]s so far discovered in Britain and one with the latest occupation beyond the [[Roman Britain|Roman period]]. The villa was built in phases from the early 2nd century to the 5th century, with the 4th-century construction transforming the building into an elite dwelling arranged around three sides of a courtyard. The 4th-century building included a heated and furnished west wing containing a dining-room (''[[triclinium]]'') with a fine [[mosaic]] floor, as well as two separate bathing suites: one for damp-heat and one for dry-heat.

The villa was discovered in 1864, and was excavated and opened to public view soon afterwards. It was acquired in 1924 by the [[National Trust]] who have conducted a long-term conservation programme, with new on-site facilities and cover-buildings.

Historians have debated whether Chedworth was a ''[[villa rustica]]'' or a religious sanctuary and hostel, as evidence has been found in support of both arguments. Most currently believe, however, that Chedworth was the former, inhabited by a very wealthy Romano-Briton.

==Siting==

The villa stands in a sheltered, shady position overlooking the [[River Coln]] in the [[Cotswolds|Cotswold Hills]] in [[Gloucestershire]]. It was located just off the Roman road known as the [[Fosse Way]], and {{cvt|8|mi}} north of the important town of [[Corinium Dobunnorum]] ([[Cirencester]]).<ref name="mccloymidgley90">{{Harvnb|McCloy|Midgley|2008|p=90}}</ref> Cirencester's reputation as a centre of tribal government and a ''civitas'' capital led to quick romanisation of the area and resulting concentration of wealth.<ref>{{Cite book|title=The Roman Villa: Chedworth|last=Goodburn|first=Roger|publisher=Curwen Press|year=1972|location=London|pages=9}}</ref> Chedworth's location in the Cotswolds and the valley of the [[River Coln]] was important for agriculture.<ref>{{Cite book|title=The Roman Villa: Chedworth|last=Goodburn|first=Roger|publisher=Curwen Press|year=1972|location=London|pages=12}}</ref> It was one of about fifty villas in the Cotswolds,<ref name="mccloymidgley90"/> and one of nine in just a {{cvt|5|mile}} radius.<ref name="mccloymidgley95">{{Harvnb|McCloy|Midgley|2008|p=95}}</ref>

The villa was deliberately located next to a natural spring in the north west corner of the complex which was the villa's main source of water, and around which was later built an apsidal shrine to the water-nymphs (''[[nymphaeum]]'').<ref name="wilson195">{{Harvnb|Wilson|2002|p=195}}</ref>

==History==
[[File:Chedworth Roman Villa 2012 - West bath house tepidarium mosaic.jpg|thumb|West bath house tepidarium mosaic]]

[[File:Mosaic floor, Chedworth - geograph.org.uk - 154259.jpg|thumb|Detail of the ''Triclinium'' mosaic: winter]]

The two nearest settlements were [[Corinium]] (Cirencester) founded as [[castra|forts]] in about 50, shortly after the Roman conquest, and [[Glevum]] (Gloucester) founded in 97. As the area became settled under Roman rule, these centres ceased to be military bases, soldiers retired to land provided by the Roman governorship in recognition of military service. It is noteworthy that twenty-two Roman villas have been found within a ten-mile radius of Chedworth. The villa may have been related to the retirement of these veteran soldiers.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Goodburn|first=Roger|url=http://worldcat.org/oclc/319670584|title=The Roman villa, Chedworth|publisher=The National Trust|year=1989|oclc=319670584}}</ref> 

The villa was founded about 120<ref name="mccloymidgley95"/> and consisted of separate buildings around 3 sides of a rectangle open to the east with a bath house to the north.<ref name="wilson191">{{Harvnb|Wilson|2002|p=191}}</ref> The original structures were typical of a working farm and outbuildings. The villa went through at least six stages of construction or re-construction.<ref name="Goodburn 1989">{{Cite book|last=Goodburn|first=Roger|url=|title=The Roman villa, Chedworth|publisher=The National Trust|year=1989|oclc=}}</ref>

In the early 3rd century (Phase II) the west and south wings were rebuilt following a fire, and the north bath suite was enlarged with extra rooms added to its eastern side.<ref name="wilson191" /> In the early 4th century (Phase III), the villa was transformed into an elite dwelling enclosing the courtyard. The existing wings were linked by a covered [[portico]], and an inner garden and outer courtyard were created.<ref name="wilson191"/> The dining-room (''[[triclinium]]'') received its [[mosaic]]s and the northern half of the west wing was converted to become a second set of baths.<ref name="wilson191"/> Shortly afterwards (Phase IIIA) the baths in the north wing were rebuilt and changed to dry-heat (''[[laconicum]]'') baths,<ref name="wilson191"/> which meant that the villa had both damp-heat and dry-heat bathing suites.<ref name="mccloymidgley95"/> The floors of at least 15 rooms were decorated with mosaics. In the late 4th century (Phase IV) the north wing was extended with the addition of a new dining-room.<ref name="wilson191"/> Many of the rooms, particularly the dining rooms were heated by ''[[hypocaust]]''.
[[File:Hypocaust_at_Chedworth_Roman_Villa.jpg|thumb|Hypocaust at Chedworth]]

A feature unique in Britain and discovered in 2017 is that a significant building phase of the villa dates from the 5th century after the [[end of Roman rule in Britain]] (410).<ref>New dating evidence at Chedworth Roman Villa - Dr Martin Papworth https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kFxInZulTV4</ref> In room 28 the mosaic and walls on the east and west sides were installed after 424.<ref>The 5th Century Chedworth Mosaic: https://archaeologynationaltrustsw.wordpress.com/tag/chedworth-roman-villa/</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Morris |first1=Steven |title=Stunning dark ages mosaic found at Roman villa in Cotswolds |url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2020/dec/10/stunning-dark-ages-mosaic-found-at-roman-villa-in-cotswolds |access-date=10 December 2020 |work=Guardian |date=10 December 2020 |archive-date=10 December 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201210000737/https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2020/dec/10/stunning-dark-ages-mosaic-found-at-roman-villa-in-cotswolds |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Chedworth Roman Villa: Mosaic's age stuns historians |work=BBC News |date=10 December 2020 |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-gloucestershire-55256415 |access-date=10 December 2020 |archive-date=10 December 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201210134800/https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-england-gloucestershire-55256415 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Britain's first known 5th century mosaic found at Chedworth Roman Villa |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/chedworth-roman-villa/features/britains-first-known-5th-century-mosaic-found-at-chedworth-roman-villa |publisher=National Trust |access-date=10 December 2020 |archive-date=10 December 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201210134758/https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/chedworth-roman-villa/features/britains-first-known-5th-century-mosaic-found-at-chedworth-roman-villa |url-status=live }}</ref>
This is the first evidence that concentrated wealth funded Roman lifestyles in Britain for at least 50 years later than previously thought, as the building of new rooms with a mosaic is evidence of prestige spending on specialized skills including mosaic craftsmen. Other mosaics in neighbouring rooms, including room 30, show stylistic similarities and may also be of the 5th century.

Later a workshop was installed on top of the mosaic floor and two hearths, made out of pieces of architecture of the villa, were built into the worn floor of the room.

==Nymphaeum==

[[File:The Nymphaeum, Chedworth Roman Villa - geograph.org.uk - 154252.jpg|thumb|Nymphaeum]]

The pool in the north-west corner of the villa complex was developed from the naturally occurring fresh-water spring which most likely inspired the location of the villa in the first place. The spring became a location for an apsidal shrine to the water-nymphs (''[[nymphaeum]]''). The extant curved rear wall is 2 metres high and is the original Roman masonry.<ref name="wilson195"/>

All of the water needs of the villa were provided for by this spring.  An octagonal pool is located at the centre and is still fed by the spring; a Christian [[chi-rho]] monogram was discovered scratched onto what was the rim of the pool.<ref name="wilson197" /> This symbol had a short presence in the early fourth century but was soon replaced by the original water nymphs.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Goodburn|first=Roger|title=The Roman Villa Chedworth|publisher=National Trust|year=1989|pages=28}}</ref>

==Temples==

[[File:Stone relief from Chedworth Roman Villa.jpg|thumb|right|Stone carving of a hunter with a dog and stag]]
Foundations of a Romano-British temple have been excavated about 800 metres south-east of the villa buildings.<ref name="pastscape327595">[http://www.pastscape.org.uk/hob.aspx?hob_id=327595 Monument No. 327595] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304111341/http://www.pastscape.org.uk/hob.aspx?hob_id=327595 |date=March 4, 2016 }}, Pastscape, retrieved 10 April 2012</ref> The remains comprise the southwest and southeast corners of a rectangular building, measuring 16.5m by 16.0m.<ref name="pastscape327595"/> Altars preserved in the villa museum probably came from the temple as did coins, glass tesserae and a stone carved niche.<ref name="pastscape327595"/>

There was, however, another Roman building in Chedworth Woods about 150 metres northwest of the villa which was destroyed in the construction of the [[Midland and South Western Junction Railway|railway]] around 1869.<ref name="pastscape327636">[http://www.pastscape.org.uk/hob.aspx?hob_id=327636 Monument No. 327636] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304071854/http://www.pastscape.org.uk/hob.aspx?hob_id=327636 |date=March 4, 2016 }}, Pastscape, retrieved 10 April 2012</ref> Finds included coins, hexagonal tiles, fragments of pillars, part of a shell-headed niche and glass tesserae.<ref name="pastscape327636"/> The stone relief of a "hunter god" with hare, dog and stag, sometimes ascribed to the southeast temple, may have come from this site.<ref name="pastscape327636"/>

Another carved figure was discovered bearing a fragmentary inscription which it is believed may refer to the healing god [[Mars (mythology)|Mars Lenus]], a deity of the [[Treveri]] tribe in [[Gaul]].<ref name="wilson197">{{Harvnb|Wilson|2002|p=197}}</ref>

==Discovery and display==

The villa was accidentally discovered in 1864 by Thomas Margetts, a gamekeeper who was digging for a ferret,<ref>{{Cite book|last=Goodburn|first=Roger|title=The Roman Villa Chedworth|publisher=National Trust|year=1989}}</ref><ref name="heritage">[http://www.theheritagetrail.co.uk/roman%20britain/chedworth_villa.htm Chedworth Roman Villa, Gloucestershire] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060503192239/http://www.theheritagetrail.co.uk/roman%20britain/chedworth_villa.htm |date=May 3, 2006 }}, Heritage Trail page, retrieved 5 April 2012</ref> and found fragments of mosaic tesserae.<ref name="crv">[http://www.chedworthromanvilla.com/ Chedworth Roman Villa] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120207111753/http://www.chedworthromanvilla.com/ |date=7 February 2012 }}, chedworthromanvilla.com, retrieved 5 April 2012</ref> The site was subsequently excavated in 1865-7 by [[James Farrer (British politician)|James Farrer]],<ref name="heritage"/> an [[antiquarian]] and the [[Member of Parliament]] for [[South Durham (UK Parliament constituency)|South Durham]]. The owner of the land was the [[Earl of Eldon]],<ref name="crv"/> and it was he who financed the excavations, roofing for the mosaics, and the building of the mock-Tudor lodge to house the artifacts.<ref name="heritage"/> Little, if anything, of the excavations was recorded. Only the best four mosaics were left exposed under shelters and the rest were reburied for their protection.<ref name="Current Archaeology, August 2015">Current Archaeology, August 2015</ref>

In 1924 the villa was acquired by the [[National Trust]].<ref name="heritage"/> Excavations have taken place periodically since then.<ref name="crv"/><ref>[http://www.pastscape.org.uk/hob.aspx?hob_id=327592 Chedworth Roman Villa] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130921060028/http://www.pastscape.org.uk/hob.aspx?hob_id=327592 |date=September 21, 2013 }}, Pastscape, retrieved 5 April 2012</ref>

In 1957-1965 Prof. [[Ian Richmond]] excavated and re-interpreted Chedworth but died in 1965 without publishing any results.<ref>Chedworth and Sir Ian's lost archive https://archaeologynationaltrustsw.wordpress.com/2013/12/01/chedworth-and-sir-ians-lost-archive/</ref> Parts of the villa were re-buried.

In 2011 a new cover building was provided for the mosaics in the west wing to ensure their preservation.<ref>[http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/home/view-page/item445474/237650/ A major transformation for Chedworth Roman Villa] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120419234900/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/home/view-page/item445474/237650/ |date=April 19, 2012 }}, National Trust, retrieved 5 April 2012</ref> A geophysical survey of the field east of the villa in 2012 revealed a central approach road running up from the valley floor and two other buildings, one a circular stone structure on the south side of the road.<ref name="Current Archaeology, August 2015"/> A new excavation campaign started in 2013 on the north wing and has revealed previously unrecorded mosaics, partially destroyed by Ian Richmond in 1964.<ref>Day 4 Beneath topsoil, Mosaic Islands, Posted on August 21, 2014 by martinpapworth, https://archaeologynationaltrustsw.wordpress.com/tag/chedworth-roman-villa/page/6/</ref>

==Geometric meander patterns==

The pavement mosaics in several rooms exhibit the typical geometric [[meander (art)|meander]] patterns found in other Roman villas throughout England. The dining room floor contains one of the most elaborate geometric designs found in the villa. Although in good condition, there are substantial portions of it missing. However, a simple mathematical algorithm has been discovered that is able to reconstruct the missing parts of the mosaic from what is still there.<ref>Liu, Y. and Toussaint, G. T. [http://cgm.cs.mcgill.ca/~godfried/teaching/dm-reading-assignments/Chedworth.pdf “Unraveling Roman mosaic meander patterns: A simple algorithm for their generation,”] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181008171439/http://cgm.cs.mcgill.ca/~godfried/teaching/dm-reading-assignments/Chedworth.pdf |date=8 October 2018 }} ''Journal of Mathematics and the Arts'', Vol. 4, Issue 1, March 2010, pp. 1-11.</ref>

==New building==

The National Trust considered that Victorian efforts at site conservation were outdated and that the early shelters were not providing sufficient protection. So since 2010 the site has been transformed.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Esmonde Cleary|first1=Simon|last2=Wood|first2=Jason|last3=Durham|first3=Emma|last4=Papworth|first4= Martin|title=Chedworth Roman Villa|journal=Current Archaeology|date=31 October 2022|publisher=The Past|location=London|url-status=live|url=https://the-past.com/feature/chedworth-roman-villa-exploring-over-150-years-of-interpretation/|access-date=14 January 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240114195400/https://the-past.com/feature/chedworth-roman-villa-exploring-over-150-years-of-interpretation/|archive-date=14 January 2024}}</ref> They appointed [[Feilden Clegg Bradley Studios]] to design a new conservation building as well as a learning facility for the archaeological site. At the same time the reception building was refurbished.
The £2.2m project was completed in March 2012.<ref name="inexhibit.com">{{Cite web|url=http://www.inexhibit.com/case-studies/roman-villa-archaeological-site-chedworth/|title=Roman Villa archaeological site Chedworth|work=Inexhibit museum magazine|access-date=28 April 2014|archive-date=10 December 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201210134736/http://www.inexhibit.com/case-studies/roman-villa-archaeological-site-chedworth/|url-status=live}}</ref>

21424615.title: Ray Island
21424615.extract: Ray Island, also known as the Ray, is a 40.5-hectare (100-acre) nature reserve west of Mersea Island in Essex. The site is a sandy hill rising out of an area of saltmarsh between Strood Channel and Ray Channel. The island is owned by the National Trust, who bought it in 1970. It was leased by the National Trust to the Essex Wildlife Trust, which managed the site. Following the cessation of the lease, the National Trust has resumed responsibility for the island's management.

'''Ray Island''', also known as '''the Ray''', is a {{convert|40.5|hectare|acre|adj=on}} nature reserve west of [[Mersea Island]] in [[Essex]]. The site is a sandy hill rising out of an area of saltmarsh between Strood Channel and Ray Channel. The island is owned by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]], who bought it in 1970.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Wild Essex site profile: Ray Island|url=https://www.wildessex.net/sites/Ray%20Island.htm|access-date=2022-02-23|website=www.wildessex.net}}</ref> It was leased by the National Trust to the [[Essex Wildlife Trust]], which managed the site. Following the cessation of the lease, the National Trust has resumed responsibility for the island's management.<ref name="EWT">{{cite web|title=Ray Island|url=http://www.essexwt.org.uk/reserves/ray-island-bonners-saltings|publisher=Essex Wildlife Trust|access-date=23 February 2022}}</ref>

==Wildlife==
The island has rough grassland and a shingle foreshore. Its flora includes saltmarsh plants such as [[Limonium humile|lax flowered sea-lavender]], [[Juncus maritimus|sea rush]] and [[golden samphire]]. Breeding birds include [[Common redshank|redshank]], [[oystercatcher]] and [[shelduck]].<ref name=EWT/>

== Environmental designations ==
The site has been designated as [[Site of Special Scientific Interest]] (SSSI), [[Marine Conservation Zone]]s (MCZ), [[Ramsar site|Ramsar Site]], [[Special Area of Conservation]] (SAC) and a [[Special Protection Area]] (SPA).<ref name="EWT" />

==Literature ==

=== ''Mehalah'' ===
Ray Island was the setting for the novel ''Mehalah: A Story of the Salt Marshes'' by [[Sabine Baring-Gould]], who was the rector of East Mersea for 10 years from 1871. Baring-Gould describes the island thus in the first chapter:

:''A more desolate region can scarce be conceived, and yet it is not without beauty. In summer, the thrift mantles the marches with shot satin, passing through all gradations of tint from maiden's blush to lily white. Thereafter a purple glow steals over the waste, as the sea lavender bursts into flower, and simultaneously every creek and pool is royally fringed with sea aster. A little later the glasswort, that shot up green and transparent as emerald glass in the early spring, turns to every tinge of carmine.''

=== The Essex Serpent ===
The marshy landscape also formed part of the inspiration for ''[[The Essex Serpent]]'', by [[Sarah Perry]].<ref name="EWT" />

=== The Turnglass ===
Ray and Mersea are the setting for ''[[The Turnglass]]'', by [[Gareth Rubin]].<ref name="EWT" />

== Folklore ==
A bear is said to have escaped from a ship onto the island and killed a group of fisherman who had landed there.

There is also the tale is of a drunkard who chased his wife and daughter into the marshes but he was drowned by the rising tide. It has been claimed that his shouts can be heard along with the panting of the mother and the baby's crying.<ref>{{Cite web|last=VMI-ADM|date=2020-11-23|title=ray island and mysterious tales {{!}} Visit Mersea Island|url=https://visitmerseaisland.co.uk/ray-island-and-mysterious-tales/|access-date=2022-02-23|language=en-GB}}</ref>

It is also claimed there is the ghost of a Roman centurion and the sound of a horse's hooves can be heard.<ref name="EWT" />

==Access==
General public access is by boat via the Ray Channel from Mersea. If using your own boat, it is important to check the state and times of the tide. Camping, barbecues and fires are banned by the trust.<ref name="EWT" /><ref name=":0" />

39044014.title: Ashleworth Tithe Barn
39044014.extract: Ashleworth Tithe Barn is a large 15th-century tithe barn located at Ashleworth, Gloucestershire, England, standing close to the River Severn. It is a Grade II* listed building, and has been scheduled as an ancient monument. It is close to, and associated with Ashleworth Court and the local Anglican church.

D. | completion_date = | demolished_date = }} '''Ashleworth Tithe Barn''' is a large 15th-century [[tithe barn]] located at [[Ashleworth]], [[Gloucestershire]], England, standing close to the [[River Severn]].{{cite web |url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/ashleworth-tithe-barn/ |title=Ashleworth Tithe Barn |accessdate=April 7, 2013 |publisher=National Trust |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130409135204/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/ashleworth-tithe-barn/ |archive-date=April 9, 2013 |url-status=live }} It is a Grade II* [[listed building]],{{cite web |title=Tithe Barn, Ashleworth Court |url=https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1171121 |website=National Heritage List for England |publisher=Historic England |accessdate=28 March 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160307031012/https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1171121 |archive-date=7 March 2016 |url-status=live }} and has been scheduled as an [[ancient monument]].{{cite web |title=Ashleworth tithe barn |url=https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1004842 |website=National Heritage List for England |publisher=Historic England |accessdate=28 March 2020}} It is close to, and associated with [[Ashleworth Court]] and the local Anglican church. ==History== The barn was built about 1500 by the canons of [[Bristol Cathedral#History of the building|St Augustine's, Bristol]] while John Newland, (1481–1515) was the [[abbot]]. A [[tithe barn]] was a type of [[Barn (building)|barn]] built in the [[Middle Ages]] for storing rents and [[tithe]]s. Farmers were required to give one-tenth of their produce to the established Church.{{cite web |title=Tithe Barns |url=http://www.tithebarns.co.uk/ |publisher=Tithe Barns |accessdate=28 March 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130817102434/http://www.tithebarns.co.uk/ |archive-date=17 August 2013 |url-status=live }} After the [[Dissolution of the Monasteries]] the barn passed into secular use.{{cite book |title=Two compotus rolls of Saint Augustine's Abbey, Bristol, for 1491-2 and 1511-12, Volume 9 |date=1938 |publisher=Bristol Record Society |pages=43–44 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aqnNAAAAMAAJ&dq=Ashleworth+Tithe+Barn+Dissolution+monasteries&pg=PA43}} In the 19th century it was converted into a barn for cows. It was acquired by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] in 1956. They have undertaken restoration work to the [[Buttress]]es and other stonework, but need to manage this to reduce the effects on the [[bat]] population which includes [[common pipistrelle]] (''Pipistrellus pipistrellus''), [[soprano pipistrelle]] (''Pipistrellus pygmaeus'') and [[Brown long-eared bat|brown long-eared]] (''Plecotus auritus'') which nest in the roof and cracks in the stonework.{{cite web |title=The project |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/ashleworth-tithe-barn/projects/conservation-repair-project |publisher=National Trust |accessdate=28 March 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160222135611/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/ashleworth-tithe-barn/projects/conservation-repair-project |archive-date=22 February 2016 |url-status=live }} ==Architecture== The [[blue lias]] [[limestone]] building is {{convert|125|ft}} long and {{convert|25|ft}} wide.{{cite web |title=Ashleworth Tithe Barn |url=http://www.greatbarns.org.uk/ashleworth_tithe_barn.html |publisher=Ken's Great Barns |accessdate=28 March 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190903113413/http://www.greatbarns.org.uk/ashleworth_tithe_barn.html |archive-date=3 September 2019 |url-status=live }} The medieval timber framed roof of the barn is of ten [[Bay (architecture)|bays]],{{cite web |title=Ashleworth |url=https://www.britainexpress.com/counties/glouces/Ashleworth.htm |publisher=Britain Express |accessdate=28 March 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170705153629/http://www.britainexpress.com/counties/glouces/Ashleworth.htm |archive-date=5 July 2017 |url-status=live }}{{cite web |title=Ashleworth History Project |url=http://www.ashleworth.btck.co.uk/VillageHistory |publisher=Ashleworth |accessdate=28 March 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190902092618/http://www.ashleworth.btck.co.uk/VillageHistory |archive-date=2 September 2019 |url-status=usurped }} and is supported by [[buttress]]es. It has a stone slate roof.{{cite web |last1=Ross |first1=David |title=Ashleworth Tithe Barn |url=https://www.britainexpress.com/counties/glouces/Ashleworth-Tithe-Barn.htm |publisher=ritain Express |accessdate=28 March 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170705172001/http://www.britainexpress.com/counties/glouces/Ashleworth-Tithe-Barn.htm |archive-date=5 July 2017 |url-status=live }} There are two porches on one side with double boarded doors. The end [[gable]]s have square holes and there are more of these in the side walls. These were to encourage [[owl]]s to enter the barn to control [[vermin]]. ==References== {{commons category|Ashleworth Tithe Barn|position=left}} {{Reflist}} [[Category:Religious buildings and structures completed in 1500]] [[Category:National Trust properties in Gloucestershire]] [[Category:Grade II* listed barns in England]] [[Category:Grade II* listed buildings in Gloucestershire]] [[Category:Scheduled monuments in Gloucestershire]]

60329341.title: Paycocke's House and Gardens
60329341.extract:
Paycocke's House and Gardens are a surviving example of a Tudor merchant's house and garden in Coggeshall, Essex, England. The house was built for Thomas Paycocke, a wealthy cloth merchant in the town. The house was very nearly destroyed in the 19th century, but was rescued and restored by Lord Noel Buxton in the early 20th century, before being handed to the care of the National Trust.
The house has been described as an attractive half-timbered house, notable particularly for its intricate woodwork and carvings.
